title: Developing new therapeutic strategies for pediatric tumors that lack clinically actionable mutations
text:
The treatment of pediatric cancers has remained largely unchanged for decades, relying primarily on
aggressive cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation, however, these therapies are often ineffective and have
debilitating long-term consequences. To address these problems, we aim to discover and validate new
pediatric-relevant synthetic-lethal drug targets, uncover compounds that block or eliminate drug-resistance cell
state transitions, and develop strategies that exploit tumor evolution to force residual drug-resistant cells into a
locally activated suicide bottleneck. We will perform the downstream experimental work and in vivo studies in
mouse models necessary to support the clinical translation of our findings, ultimately aiming to improve cure
rates and long-term quality of life for children with high-risk cancers.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring of Bacterial Pathogens of Veterinary Concern
text:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring is a critical function for veterinary
diagnostic laboratories to aid in identification of new or emerging resistance, to identify
potential resistance reservoirs, and assess efficacy of interventions to reduce resistance
development. Not only do resistant bacterial infections impact animal health and welfare, but
they also have significant potential for causing negative human health consequences through
transmission of resistant bacteria or resistance genes through food or animal contact. Whole
genome sequence AMR data form important veterinary bacterial pathogens and improvements
in standardized data quality assurance/quality control for bacterial resistance detection
increases the ability of FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine to accurately detect resistance and
provide more accurate monitoring of antimicrobial resistance in veterinary species.

title: The Cytoskeletal Drivers of Cell Polarity
text:
The creation of polarized structures within cells is a requirement for essential elements of life such as cell
division and differentiation. This proposal aims to elucidate how cells precisely control the structural
components that define cell shape by examining the proteins that regulate the cytoskeleton. Understanding
these processes is crucial, as disruption to the organization of the cytoskeleton, polarity, and cell structure is a
contributing factor to numerous diseases including cancer.

title: Cancer Risk, Detection & Interception
text: The Cancer Risk, Detection, and Interception Research Program (CRDI) at the Duke Cancer Institute (DCI) is a new multidisciplinary program, launched in 2021, that combines a strong translational science approach with population health science by emphasizing the pre-malignant and early-cancer space as an important time for active intervention. The CRDI Program, led by Meira Epplein, PhD and Katherine Garman, MD, centers around three Specific Aims: 1) To identify novel environmental and biological markers for cancer risk assessment; 2) To improve detection of pre-malignant and early-stage disease; and 3) To advance cancer interception through development of interventions in pre-malignant and early-stage disease. Across all aims, CRDI focuses on the importance of social elements of health, access to health care, and health disparities, and prioritizes community engagement and representation in our research projects. CRDI’s research is also highly relevant to DCI’s Catchment Area (CA) priorities, including lung, prostate, breast, colorectal and gastric cancer. As our new program developed, we identified several focus areas highly relevant to our aims including: Cancer Genetics and Genomics, Environmental Exposures and Cancer Risk; the Pre-Cancer Microenvironment; Cancer Epidemiology and Cancer Disparities; and Aging and Cancer (including senescence). CRDI Program accomplishments since its inception include: 1) research across all three aims targeting CA priorities, including five R01/R01 equivalents in breast cancer, three R01s in prostate cancer, and five R01s (including an R37 Merit Award) in gastrointestinal cancers; 2) strong focus on cancer disparities, including six NCI-funded grants; 3) ground-breaking work in cancer interception with leadership of the Prevention of Progression to Pancreatic Cancer Trial and the Breast Pre-Cancer Atlas Center; 4) significant outreach and educational activities with community partners focused on gastrointestinal cancer interception and early detection; and 5) novel work evaluating local firefighters’ exposure to carcinogenic chemicals. CRDI is comprised of 33 full members from 11 departments and 4 schools within Duke University. Total direct funding for full program members is $8.2M, of which $6.4M is peer reviewed, including $4.3M from the NCI. Since the inception of the program in 2021 through 2023, program members published 636 cancer focused papers, 93 (15%) are intra-programmatic, 276 (43%) are inter-programmatic collaborations and 147 (23%) are impact factor over 10. Since the inception of the program in 2021 through 2023, the program enrolled 1,724 participants to all trials and 444 to interventional trials. CRDI is a novel, paradigm-shifting program that focuses on fostering collaborations and translating basic and population health science; CRDI is positioned to positively impact clinical practice and health policy by emphasizing the critical time period of pre-malignant disease and early cancer when active intervention can improve outcomes.

title: Testing the Pain Relief of musculOskeletal conditions and Arthritis using Carefully Tailored InterVEntions (PROACTIVE) Intervention: A Randomized Controlled Trial
text:
Chronic musculoskeletal pain, while a leading cause of disablement, is a neglected public health issue in aging
communities. Specifically, chronic musculoskeletal pain is primarily driven by movement-evoked pain which
contributes to pronounced mobility limitations and disability in adults in later life. Disrupting persistent patterns
in this population demands novel focused self-management interventions that will attenuate the adverse
economic, functional, and mental health consequences associated with chronic musculoskeletal pain.

title: Gamma delta T cell based melanoma therapies
text:
This project leverages our humanized mouse models to achieve two goals: 1) Determine treatment efficacy of
adoptive γδT cell transfer for melanoma. 2) Stimulate endogenous γδT cells for melanoma therapy. We
expect that HuMice will allow us to test Vγ9Vδ2+ T cells-based cancer therapy for the first time in a suitable
model system and our new therapies are effective and may be optimized and tested in future clinical trials.

title: Regulatory Mechanisms of Gasdermin-mediated Pyroptosis
text:
Pyroptosis is an inflammatory form of programmed cell death mediated by the gasdermins and is
implicated in numerous diseases including allergy and autoimmune disorders, infectious diseases, metabolic
disorders, and cancer. The molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis
remain to be established. Using a combination of molecular biology, multi-omics approaches, and live cell
imaging, our research program will define the regulatory mechanisms of gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis which
can open doors for the development of novel therapeutics for pyroptosis-related diseases.

title: POI-KB: Design and Development of a Knowledgebase for Accelerating Perioperative Organ Injury Research and Translation
text:
We will develop a knowledgebase for perioperative organ injury (POI) which aims to catalogue and curate POI
information available in public data resources and bridge the multidisciplinary and translational gap with an
eventual goal of improving perioperative outcome.

title: Impact of PIGA Loss on Hematopoietic Stem Cell Function
text:
Hematopoietic stem cells can develop gene mutations that alter their function and lead to blood diseases. One
such blood disease, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), is caused by acquired mutations in the PIGA
gene, which allows mutant cells to outgrow normal hematopoietic cells, causing hemolytic anemia and
thrombosis. Recently, we found differences in the function of PIGA-mutated hematopoietic stem cells and will
now build on these studies to determine mechanisms responsible for the emergence of PIGA-mutant cells in
order to improve PNH treatment.

title: Defining mechanisms to promote antitumor immunity by modulating one-carbon metabolism
text:
This project will probe the transformative idea that enhancing one carbon (1C) metabolism will
increase anti-tumor immune functions and synergize with ICB. We will define how formate and
1C metabolism improve T cell function to synergize with PD-1 blockade, and identify metabolic
pathways downstream of 1C metabolism that enhance T cell functions. These studies will
illuminate mechanisms by which 1C metabolism and metabolic support with formate enhance ICB,
and identify novel targets and strategies for improving cancer immunotherapy outcomes.

title: Investigating the neutrophil-sensory neuron crosstalk in lung cancer
text:
Nerves are found in many types of solid tumors; however, tumor innervation has long been viewed
as passive bystanders in cancer. Although increased innervation is associated with aggressive
tumor phenotype and poor prognosis in cancer patients, the underlying biology of these clinical
associations has been elusive. Our research aims to develop an in-depth and broad
understanding of neuro-immune interactions in cancer with a particular focus on the bi-directional
crosstalk between the nociceptive sensory neurons and the tumor microenvironment (TME), and
to explore whether we can target such interactions for more effective cancer treatment.

title: Organoid and Primary Culture Core
text: CORE 2: ORGANOID AND HUMAN CELL CULTURE CORE SUMMARY The Organoid and Human Cell Culture Core is a critical component of the Gladstone PhAIge Therapy Center, designed to accelerate the clinical development of phage-based therapeutics targeting ESKAPE pathogens, with a particular focus on Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp). Antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health crisis, contributing to over a million deaths annually. Phage therapy represents a promising solution to this challenge, especially as the discovery of antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action continues to lag. However, the lack of advanced preclinical models that adequately replicate human physiology and host responses hinders the translation of phage therapy to clinical use. The Organoid and Human Cell Culture Core will address this unmet need by developing and implementing cutting-edge ex vivo human cell culture systems, including 3D human airway organoids (HAOs), 2D air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures, and other primary cell models. These models offer significant advantages over traditional in vitro models by closely mimicking the complexity of human lung tissues, including cellular diversity, barrier integrity, and innate immune responses, enabling more precise evaluation of phage efficacy and safety in a clinically relevant context. The Core will accomplish this goal in two specific aims. Aim 1 focuses on establishing robust infection models for Kp in 3D HAOs and 2D ALI cultures and leveraging high-throughput sequencing-based assays to assess phage adsorption, entry efficiency, and specificity to support Project 1. By identifying phages with high on-target effects against bacteria and minimal off-target effects on human cells, this aim will streamline the selection of optimal candidates for clinical development. Aim 2 will evaluate mammalian host responses to phage therapy, including bacterial clearance, epithelial damage, host cell viability, Kp strain variation, and inflammatory cytokine expression, a critical step to advance the most promising phage cocktails to future clinical trials. The Core will also incorporate patient-derived organoids, including those from individuals with cystic fibrosis, to investigate how pre-existing epithelial dysfunction affects therapeutic outcomes. The Core leverages Dr. Melanie Ott’s recognized expertise in organoid technology, with a proven track record of using HAOs to model infectious diseases, including SARS-CoV-2, HCV, HIV, and influenza. This foundational expertise, applied to Kp infections, will help develop rigorous quantitative assays to evaluate phage efficacy and safety independent from human donor bias. By integrating human models into the Center’s research pipeline in Projects 1–2 and the Advanced Computational Core, the Organoid and Human Cell Culture Core will accelerate the translation of phage therapies from bench to bedside.

title: Improving Outcomes for Patients with Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
text:
IMPROVING OUTCOMES FOR PATIENTS WITH AR-DEPENDENT TRIPLE-
NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER
Despite recent advances in treating triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) with chemo-immunotherapy, patients
whose tumors depend on the androgen receptor (AR) protein derive little benefit from these new approaches.
To address this critical gap, the proposed research will investigate AR inhibitors in a pre-surgical TNBC clinical
trial to define their impact on standard-of-care therapy, while concurrently discovering biomarkers predictive of
AR antagonist response and developing an improved diagnostic test to accurately identify patients with AR-
dependent tumors. These advancements are crucial for developing new therapeutic strategies for TNBC patients
with AR-dependent tumors who currently lack effective treatment options.

title: Diverse visual processing properties of novel ganglion cell and amacrine cell types in the human retina
text:
The goal of the proposed work is to understand how the diverse cell types in the human retina process visual
information and transmit it to the brain, and how this compares to the large existing body of work from the
closest animal model. Using a collection of novel techniques, we are now able to study the functioning of
retinas obtained from human donors. This work will make it possible to understand the function of the human
retina in ways that were never before possible, with implications ranging from understanding human vision to
diagnosing visual disorders and developing retinal implants to treat incurable blindness.

title: Deep Learning of Snoring to Predict Collapse Site, Treatment Outcomes, and its Clinical Translation in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
text:
Successful Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) treatment requires the understanding of the potential site of 
collapse, which range from vellum to epiglottis, during sleep. 
This project uses deep learning to analyze existing snoring and sleep-study data to identify where the airway 
collapses and to predict which patients will respond best to specific treatments. 
By developing a non-invasive, low-cost snore based approach for personalized therapy selection, this work will 
help improve OSA treatment management.

title: Identification of attenuating mutations in the envelope protein for the rational design of a candidate West Nile live-attenuated vaccine.
text:
Project Narrative. West Nile virus (WNV) is the most common mosquito-borne orthoflavivirus in the
United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has identified WNV vaccine
development as a public health priority, particularly the need for a live-attenuated vaccine (LAV) that
provides protection with a single dose. This project aims to identify mutations in the envelope (E)
protein to support the rational design of a candidate LAV for WNV.

title: Assessing how ocular surface nerves, immune cells, and epithelial cells communicate to encourage neuro-immune homeostasis
text:
The links between ocular surface innervation and disease are apparent; however, there is a wide gap in the
understanding how ocular surface nerves may affect and may be affected by disease. This proposal is
designed to create large “-omic” data sets that morphologically, anatomically, molecularly, and functionally
characterize interactions between ocular surface nerves, epithelial cells, and immune cells during ocular
surface health and disease

title: Anti-CV2 autoantibodies unmask a CRMP5/GluN2B pain signaling hub
text:
It is now well accepted that neuroimmune interactions contribute to abnormal pain states. One such rare
neurological condition is Paraneoplastic Syndrome where a peripheral tumor can trigger an immune response
against a neuronal auto-antigen. This proposal will explore the molecular, biochemical and functional relation of
a neuronal auto-antigen to pain

title: Decoupling reproductive and somatic aging using novel C. elegans technology
text:
Our Leica DMi8 microscope recently sustained substantial water damage during
microﬂuidic imaging experiments conducted by my PhD student. Worm incubation media
leaked and damaged the z-axis controller as well as several additional components.
Because this repair expense resulted from an unforeseen incident, it was not included in the
original budget for our awarded R15 grant. The requested funds will therefore be used to
repair our inverted microscope.

title: Methylglyoxal-mediated activation of the integrated stress response promotes eIF2A-dependent translation in diabetic neuropathic pain
text:
Our project aims to elucidate how methylglyoxal-induced integrated stress response activation drives diabetic
neuropathic pain (DNP) through eIF2A-dependent translational mechanisms, employing advanced sequencing
(TRAP-seq, Ribo-seq), gene-editing (CRISPR-Cas9), and functional assays in mouse, rat, and human primary
nociceptors. By critically assessing cross-species connections, we will improve the accuracy of preclinical
models, ensuring greater relevance to human diabetic neuropathy. Ultimately, this integrative approach will
yield rigorously validated molecular targets, transforming diagnostics and therapeutic strategies for DNP.
